title: Rashi's daughters
hook: tradition remembers them as learned; his grandsons began the Tosafist school

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rashi's life: a teacher in Troyes, by tradition a man of the vineyards, whose commentary still sits beside the text. Your line was vintner and teacher. What did you carry through your workday? Today, the people at his table. Day nine hundred thirty-five.

Rashi had daughters, tradition says, and no sons. One answer to a legal question, preserved under his name, stops partway through for an apology. The writer is weak and ill, he says, and cannot hold the pen himself; his daughter is writing down his words. That is how tradition reads it. A teacher in bed, and a daughter at the desk, taking down the law in her own hand. Through his daughters, his learning went on to the next generation and the one after that. Today, Rashi's daughters.
screen: `A LETTER FROM TROYES.` → `HIS DAUGHTER HOLDS THE PEN.` → `LEARNING PASSES THROUGH THEM.`

segments.voice: Tradition remembers their names as Yocheved, Miriam and Rachel. We have very little written by them or about them directly, and that silence is worth saying out loud: what women in that world knew and taught was often never written down. What we do know is the family that grew around them. Yocheved married Meir, one of Rashi's students. Their sons became great teachers in their own right. One was Samuel, known as the Rashbam, who wrote his own commentary on the Torah and was not shy about reading a verse differently from his grandfather. Another was Jacob, known as Rabbeinu Tam, a great teacher of law in France. These grandsons and their students began a new way of learning the Talmud. They called their notes tosafot, additions. Where Rashi explained a passage line by line, the Tosafists asked: how does this line fit with that one, in another tractate? They raised contradictions and worked them out, generation after generation, in schools across France and Germany. Open a printed page of the Talmud today: Rashi on the inner margin, the Tosafot on the outer margin, the grandfather facing the school his grandsons began, across the text. And then there are the stories. A popular one says Rashi's daughters wore tefillin. It is told and retold, but no early source says so. So tell the story as a story. The thing the sources do show is quieter, and real: a house where learning ran through the daughters to the grandsons, and a daughter who, tradition says, could take down her father's legal answers when he could not.
screen: `YOCHEVED, MIRIAM, RACHEL.` · `GRANDSONS: RASHBAM AND RABBEINU TAM.` · then, large: `TOSAFOT: ADDITIONS.` · `A STORY IS NOT A SOURCE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: encourage a girl to learn. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind a girl or young woman in your life: a daughter, a niece, a student, a neighbor's kid, a younger coworker. Think of one thing she's curious about. Picture handing her something: a book, a question, an hour of your time, a word that says her mind is worth training. If no one comes to mind, think of the girls you went to school with, and what someone could have said to them. If you pray, you can hold her in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Rashi's daughters. Remembered by tradition as learned; through them came grandsons who began the Tosafot, the additions printed opposite their grandfather on the Talmud page. Today's word.
Your line: daughters of learning. Today, tell one girl or young woman that her questions are worth asking, and answer one of them. Day nine hundred thirty-five.
